title: Indian Startup Astrobase Unveils Everest, the Country's First Full-Flow Rocket Engine
excerpt: Bangalore-based Astrobase Space Technologies is developing an 800 kN methane-fueled engine modeled on SpaceX's Raptor, with a maiden orbital launch targeted for 2029.
body:
• Astrobase is building India's first privately developed Full-Flow Staged Combustion (FFSC) methane engine, a cycle only SpaceX has ever flown
  • The 800 kN engine will power a reusable medium-lift rocket with seven engines clustered under a four-metre booster
  • The company secured IN-SPACe Technology Adoption Fund support in June 2026 for its indigenous propulsion programme
  • A maiden orbital launch is targeted for 2029, supporting India's goal of a $44 billion space economy by 2034

Astrobase Space Technologies, a Bangalore-based startup founded in 2024 by former ISRO engineers and industry veterans, has emerged as one of India's most ambitious private space ventures with its development of the Everest engine — the country's first full-flow staged combustion (FFSC) rocket engine.

The Everest of Propulsion Systems

The FFSC cycle is widely considered the most complex engine architecture ever built. Unlike conventional staged combustion, it requires two pre-burners instead of one, converting all propellant into hot gas before it enters the combustion chamber. The result: extreme chamber pressures exceeding 300 bar, top-tier efficiency, and engines capable of hundreds of reuses.

Only one FFSC engine has ever flown — SpaceX's Raptor. Globally, just seven engines of this type have been run on a test stand, according to Indian Defence News. ISRO itself has never attempted the cycle, making Astrobase's effort a significant leap for India's private space sector.

""Scaling up technology also would require money."

The company's 800 kN LOX-methane engine is designed to power a reusable medium-lift launch vehicle in a seven-engine configuration similar to SpaceX's Falcon 9. The first stage is engineered for recovery and reuse, addressing India's launch bottlenecks for satellite constellation deployments.

Government Backing and Infrastructure

In June 2026, Astrobase secured a major boost when the Indian National Space Promotion and Authorization Centre (IN-SPACe) selected it for support under its Technology Adoption Fund. The grant agreement, tied to defined technical milestones, was signed by co-founder and CEO Neeraj Khandelwal during a ceremony attended by Commerce Minister Piyush Goyal.

"Scaling up technology also would require money. We need to have more and more investments coming in domestically, internationally, whether in the form of philanthropy, from foundations, from business players."

— Jitendra Singh, Union Minister

Astrobase has already built substantial infrastructure. The company operates a 21.5-acre propulsion test facility in Anantapur, Andhra Pradesh, equipped with a 200-ton thrust stand — India's first private high-thrust LOX-methane test site. A 46,000-square-foot assembly and integration facility in Bangalore handles end-to-end design and manufacturing.

Milestones and Road Ahead

In September 2025, Astrobase conducted a successful sub-scale hot-fire test on its first attempt, validating combustion stability, materials, and flow systems. In March 2026, the company received India's largest 3D printer at its Bangalore facility, delivered on four heavy-duty trucks, to establish a dedicated production line for its FFSC engines.

Full-scale engine trials are currently underway, with the engine under hot-fire testing at the Anantapur facility. The company is targeting a maiden orbital launch by 2029.

As India works toward building a $44 billion space economy by 2034, Astrobase's development represents a critical step in strengthening indigenous space infrastructure capabilities and reducing dependence on foreign launch services.
nri_angle: Astrobase's SpaceX-rivaling engine positions India as a serious competitor in global commercial spaceflight, a point of pride for the diaspora and a potential draw for NRI investment in India's $44 billion space economy.
